title: CS161 08: PRNGs and Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange

questions.q: In cryptography, what does 'random' usually mean?
choices: Random and unpredictable
Any non-deterministic outcome, even a heavily biased one
Produced by a physical process rather than an algorithm
Evenly spaced across a range of values
questions.explain: Cryptographic randomness has to be unpredictable. A coin that lands heads 99% of the time is random, but it is easy to guess, so it is a poor source for keys.

questions.q: A coin that lands heads 99% of the time has high entropy, because each flip is still a random event.
questions.explain: Entropy measures uncertainty, or surprise. You can nearly always predict the biased coin, so its entropy is low. A fair coin has high entropy.

questions.q: Which distribution produces the greatest entropy?
choices: The uniform distribution (all outcomes equally likely)
A distribution heavily weighted toward one outcome
A normal (bell-curve) distribution
Any distribution, as long as the samples come from a physical source
questions.explain: The uniform distribution has the most entropy. That is why we ideally want crypto randomness to be uniformly random bits, like fair coin tosses.

questions.q: Which of these could serve as sources of true randomness?
choices: An unpredictable circuit on a CPU
Random noise signals
The microsecond at which a user presses a key
The output of HMAC-DRBG
A counter that increments once per second
questions.explain: True randomness comes from sampling unpredictable physical processes. HMAC-DRBG is deterministic, so its output is pseudorandom, and a counter is completely predictable.

questions.q: Why do systems use pseudorandomness instead of drawing true randomness every time an algorithm needs random bits?
choices: True, unbiased randomness is computationally expensive to generate
Pseudorandom bits have more entropy than truly random bits
Truly random bits cannot be used as cryptographic keys
Pseudorandom bits are non-deterministic, so they are harder to reproduce
questions.explain: True randomness has to be sampled from physical processes, which is expensive and can be biased. A pRNG stretches a small amount of it into many bits that look random.

questions.q: What is the term for pseudorandom bits that no efficient algorithm can tell apart from truly random bits? (two words)
questions.explain: A good pseudorandom algorithm produces output that is computationally indistinguishable from true random bits. No efficient attacker can tell the difference.

questions.q: What is the name for the initial truly random input given to a pRNG?
questions.explain: A pRNG takes a small truly random seed and outputs a long sequence of pseudorandom bits.

questions.q: Two people who run the same pRNG algorithm with the same seed will get the same output.
questions.explain: pRNGs are deterministic. This is exactly what lets a pRNG-based stream cipher decrypt: the receiver regenerates the same bits.

questions.q: An attacker with unlimited computing power sees output from a pRNG that uses an n-bit seed. How could they tell it apart from truly random bits?
choices: Run the pRNG on all 2^n possible seeds and check whether any of them produces the observed output
Check whether 0s and 1s appear equally often
They can't. pRNG output is perfectly indistinguishable even with unlimited computation
Invert the pRNG's output to recover the seed in polynomial time
questions.explain: A pRNG is only computationally indistinguishable. Brute-forcing all 2^n seeds tells it apart, but that is infeasible under any practical limit on computation.

questions.q: Why does a pRNG maintain internal state instead of outputting a fixed number of bits per seed?
choices: So it can generate as many pseudorandom bits as needed, on demand, without needing new true randomness each time
So it can return the original seed to the caller later
So that its output becomes non-deterministic
So that an attacker who learns the state still cannot predict future output
questions.explain: The state is updated on each Generate or seeding call, so a single seed can produce output indefinitely. Learning the state does let an attacker predict future output.

questions.q: Which functions make up the formal definition of a pRNG?
choices: Seed(entropy)
Reseed(entropy)
Generate(n)
Rollback(n)
Verify(output)
questions.explain: Seed initializes the internal state, Reseed mixes in more entropy, and Generate outputs n pseudorandom bits while updating the state.

questions.q: Which pRNG function outputs pseudorandom bits and also updates the internal state?
choices: Generate(n)
Seed(entropy)
Reseed(entropy)
None of them. Output never changes the state
questions.explain: Generate(n) returns n pseudorandom bits and updates the state. Some pRNGs also let it take extra entropy. Seed and Reseed only take in entropy and set or update the state.

questions.q: An attacker learns a pRNG's internal state right after bit 100 is generated. If the pRNG is rollback-resistant, what can the attacker learn about bits 1 through 100?
choices: Nothing. Those earlier bits remain computationally indistinguishable from random
Only the most recently generated bit
All of them, but none of the future bits
Only the bits generated since the last reseed
questions.explain: Rollback resistance means that knowing the current state reveals nothing about earlier output.

questions.q: A system uses one pRNG to generate a secret key first and then to generate IVs. The pRNG is NOT rollback-resistant, and an attacker compromises its state after the IVs are generated. What is most at risk?
choices: The secret key that was generated earlier
Only the IVs, which are public anyway
Nothing, because secure pRNG output is indistinguishable from random
Only future output, never past output
questions.explain: Without rollback resistance, the attacker can work backward from the compromised state to earlier output, which here is the secret key.

questions.q: Any pRNG whose output is indistinguishable from random (to someone who doesn't know the seed) is automatically rollback-resistant.
questions.explain: Rollback resistance is an extra property. It covers what happens after the state is compromised, and not every secure pRNG has it.

questions.q: Why is HMAC-DRBG rollback-resistant?
choices: Computing the previous state from the current state would mean reversing the underlying hash function
It resets K and V to 0 after every Generate call
It deletes the seed right after initialization
It reseeds with true randomness after every output block
questions.explain: The state is updated with HMAC, which is built on a one-way hash. Going backward would require inverting the hash.

questions.q: Viewed as pRNGs, AES-CTR and ChaCha20 lack rollback resistance.
questions.explain: Their internal state is the key plus a counter. Anyone with that state can set the counter back and recompute earlier output. That same ability to jump around is what makes them useful as stream ciphers.

questions.q: HMAC-DRBG's internal state has two values, K and V. What role does each play?
choices: K is the HMAC key and V is the HMAC message input
K is the seed and V is the output buffer
K is the HMAC message input and V is the HMAC key
K is a counter and V is the IV
questions.explain: K is used as the secret HMAC key, and V is the message that gets HMACed.

questions.q: Inside the Generate(n) loop of HMAC-DRBG, how is each new block of output produced?
choices: V = HMAC(K, V), then V is appended to the output
V = HMAC(V, K), then K is appended to the output
K = HMAC(K, counter), then K is appended to the output
output = HMAC(seed, n)
questions.explain: Each block is the HMAC of the previous block. The loop repeats until there are at least n bits, and output[0:n] is returned.

questions.q: Why is HMAC-DRBG's output indistinguishable from random?
choices: It is essentially many HMAC outputs, and HMAC output looks random to anyone who doesn't know the key K
It mixes fresh true randomness into every output block
The 0x00 and 0x01 constants make the output uniform
It encrypts each block with AES before outputting it
questions.explain: As long as the internal state, including K, stays secret, HMAC output cannot be told apart from random. HMAC-DRBG's output is just a chain of HMAC outputs.

questions.q: HMAC-DRBG uses an HMAC with 256-bit output. Generate(600) is called with no additional entropy. How many HMAC calls are made in total, counting the state update at the end?
questions.explain: The loop runs until the output is at least 600 bits: 256, 512, 768, so 3 HMAC calls. The state update afterward adds 2 more: K = HMAC(K, V || 0x00) and V = HMAC(K, V). 3 + 2 = 5.

questions.q: Same HMAC-DRBG (256-bit HMAC output), but now Generate(600) is called WITH additional true random input s. How many HMAC calls are made in total?
questions.explain: Producing 600 bits still takes 3 HMAC calls. With extra input the state update has 4 calls: K = HMAC(K, V||s||0x00), V = HMAC(K, V), K = HMAC(K, V||s||0x01), V = HMAC(K, V). 3 + 4 = 7.

questions.q: How does HMAC-DRBG's Reseed differ from its Seed?
choices: Reseed does not reset K and V to 0 first. Otherwise the steps are the same
Reseed produces output bits, while Seed does not
Reseed skips the step that uses 0x01
Reseed replaces K directly with the new entropy
questions.explain: Seed starts by setting K = 0 and V = 0. Reseed skips that and mixes the new entropy into the existing state with the same HMAC steps.

questions.q: Your seed source is so biased that each bit carries only 0.2 bits of entropy. How many bits of seed material must you feed HMAC-DRBG for its internal state to get 128 bits of actual entropy?
questions.explain: 128 / 0.2 = 640. HMAC-DRBG hashes the seed, so it accepts seeds of any length and gathers the entropy spread across them.

questions.q: Mixing a string with no entropy (such as all zero bits or the digits of pi) into HMAC-DRBG's seed material makes its internal state weaker.
questions.explain: Adding zero-entropy strings does not make the internal state worse. It just adds no new unpredictability.

questions.q: What does DRBG stand for in HMAC-DRBG?
questions.explain: DRBG = Deterministic Random Bit Generator. It is deterministic given its seed, like any pRNG.

questions.q: How does a pRNG-based stream cipher encrypt a message?
choices: It XORs the plaintext with pRNG output, using that output as a one-time pad
It splits the plaintext into fixed-size blocks and applies a pseudorandom permutation to each
It hashes the plaintext together with the key
It uses the plaintext as the pRNG's seed
questions.explain: The pRNG generates a pseudorandom keystream, and each plaintext bit is XORed with the matching keystream bit.

questions.q: In a pRNG-based stream cipher, what is the secret key?
choices: The seed used to seed the pRNG
The IV
The first block of pRNG output
The ciphertext's last block
questions.explain: The secret key is the seed. Alice and Bob seed the same pRNG with it, so they get the same keystream.

questions.q: Why do Alice and Bob seed the pRNG with a random IV in addition to their secret key?
choices: So the pRNG output is different for each message, which avoids reusing the one-time pad
So the ciphertext is shorter than the plaintext
Because the pRNG cannot be seeded with the key alone
So that the IV can be kept secret as a second key
questions.explain: Without an IV, the same key would give the same keystream every time, which is key reuse. A fresh random IV makes each keystream different and unpredictable. The IV is sent in the clear.

questions.q: Which is the correct encryption for a pRNG-based stream cipher with key K and message M?
choices: Enc(K, M) = <IV, PRNG(K, IV) XOR M>
Enc(K, M) = <IV, PRNG(K) XOR M XOR IV>
Enc(K, M) = <IV, PRNG(M, IV) XOR K>
Enc(K, M) = <PRNG(K, IV), IV XOR M>
questions.explain: The ciphertext is the IV plus the keystream PRNG(K, IV) XORed with M. To decrypt, compute PRNG(K, IV) XOR C2.

questions.q: An encrypted file is being downloaded. What can a stream cipher do here that a block cipher mode typically cannot?
choices: Decrypt each bit as soon as it arrives, without waiting for a full block
Decrypt without knowing the key
Detect whether the file was tampered with
Shrink the file while decrypting it
questions.explain: Stream ciphers work bit by bit as data arrives. Block ciphers may need a whole block, several blocks, or the entire message before they can decrypt.

questions.q: You want to read only the last few bytes of a 1 TB encrypted file. Why is AES-CTR or ChaCha20 much better for this than using HMAC-DRBG as a stream cipher?
choices: Their keystream includes a counter, so you can jump straight to the right position
HMAC-DRBG's output is not indistinguishable from random
AES-CTR and ChaCha20 are rollback-resistant, but HMAC-DRBG is not
HMAC-DRBG can only generate 256 bits per seed
questions.explain: With a counter you set it to the target position and decrypt just those bytes. HMAC-DRBG would have to compute about 1 TB of output from the start before it reached the end.

questions.q: Bob can decrypt a pRNG-based stream cipher because the pRNG is deterministic: the same key and IV produce the same pseudorandom bits Alice used.
questions.explain: Bob regenerates PRNG(K, IV) and XORs it with the ciphertext. XORing the keystream a second time cancels it out and recovers the plaintext.

questions.q: About how much total ciphertext can you encrypt under one key before AES-CTR's keystream stops being effectively indistinguishable from pRNG output?
choices: About 2^64 bits
About 2^32 bits
About 2^128 bits
There is no limit
questions.explain: AES is a pseudorandom permutation, not a generator. As long as the total under one key stays around 2^64 bits, its keystream works effectively like pRNG output.

questions.q: What is a one-way function?
choices: Given x, f(x) is easy to compute, but given y it is practically impossible to find an x with f(x) = y
A function that only the holder of a secret key can compute
A function that can be inverted easily, but only once
A function that maps every input to the same output
questions.explain: Easy forward, infeasible backward. It's like turning a cow into hamburger: you can't get the cow back.

questions.q: Given g^x mod p (with p a large prime and g a generator), recovering x is believed to be hard. What is this problem called?
questions.explain: This is the discrete logarithm problem. No efficient algorithm for it is known, which makes f(x) = g^x mod p a candidate one-way function.

questions.q: In the paint-mixing analogy for Diffie-Hellman, what assumption makes the scheme secure?
choices: Mixing colors is easy, but separating a mixture back into its colors is practically impossible
The common public color is kept secret from Eve
Eve cannot see the paint mixtures being exchanged
Alice and Bob choose the same secret color
questions.explain: Mixing corresponds to the easy direction of a one-way function. The common color is public, and Eve sees every mixture that is exchanged.

questions.q: In the paint analogy, why doesn't Eve get the shared secret just by mixing the green-amber and green-blue mixtures she saw?
choices: The result has the common green in it twice (green-amber-green-blue), so it isn't green-amber-blue
Mixing two mixtures is computationally impossible
Eve never sees the green-blue mixture
The shared secret contains no green at all
questions.explain: Combining the two public values doubles the common component. The math version: multiplying g^a and g^b gives g^(a+b), not g^(ab).

questions.q: Which technique makes computing g^x mod p efficient when x is known?
choices: Repeated squaring
Trying every exponent until the result matches
Factoring p
Brute-forcing g
questions.explain: Repeated squaring computes modular exponentiation quickly. That is the easy direction of the one-way function.

questions.q: For a 2048-bit prime p, the fastest known algorithms for computing g^(ab) mod p from g^a mod p, g^b mod p, g, and p are fast enough for practical attacks.
questions.explain: The best known algorithms take about 2^(c n^(1/3) (log n)^(2/3)) time for an n-bit prime. At n = 2048 that is far too slow for any reasonable attack.

questions.q: In a Diffie-Hellman exchange between Alice and Bob, which values can an eavesdropper Eve see?
choices: p
g
A = g^a mod p
B = g^b mod p
a
The shared secret S = g^(ab) mod p
questions.explain: p and g are public parameters, and A and B are sent openly. The exponents a and b are never sent, and Eve cannot feasibly compute S from what she sees.

questions.q: Toy Diffie-Hellman: p = 11, g = 2. Alice's secret is a = 3. What value A does Alice send to Bob?
questions.explain: A = g^a mod p = 2^3 mod 11 = 8.

questions.q: Toy Diffie-Hellman: p = 11, g = 2, Alice's secret a = 3, Bob's secret b = 4. What shared secret S do they compute?
questions.explain: A = 2^3 mod 11 = 8 and B = 2^4 mod 11 = 5. Alice computes B^a = 5^3 = 125 mod 11 = 4. Bob computes A^b = 8^4 = 4096 mod 11 = 4.

questions.q: Alice has her secret a and has received Bob's B = g^b mod p. How does she compute the shared secret?
choices: B^a mod p
A^b mod p
A * B mod p
g^(a+b) mod p
questions.explain: B^a = (g^b)^a = g^(ab) mod p. Alice can't compute A^b because she doesn't know b. A*B mod p equals g^(a+b), which is the wrong value.

questions.q: Diffie-Hellman is usually used to create an ephemeral key. What does 'ephemeral' mean here?
choices: The key is used for a series of encryptions and decryptions, then discarded once it is no longer needed
The key is published for anyone to use
The key is reused across every session for years
The key is derived from a password
questions.explain: Ephemeral keys are temporary. Diffie-Hellman essentially lets two parties agree on a fresh random value even with an eavesdropper listening.

questions.q: In practice, what is done to the shared value S before it is used as a symmetric key?
choices: It is passed through a hash function
It is sent to the other party for confirmation
It is reduced modulo g
Nothing. S is always used directly
questions.explain: For technical reasons, a hash function is applied to S, and the hash output is used as the shared key.

questions.q: On a network, each participant picks a secret x and publishes X = g^x mod p ahead of time. When two participants want to talk, how much work does each one do to get their shared key?
choices: One modular exponentiation
A brute-force search over all exponents
A full new exchange, including choosing new p and g
Nothing, because the shared key is published too
questions.explain: Each looks up the other's public value Y and computes Y^x mod p. Choosing p, g, x, and X can all be done in advance.

questions.q: The parameters p and g must be kept secret between Alice and Bob for Diffie-Hellman to be secure.
questions.explain: p and g are public. They are often hardcoded or set by a standard, and they don't have to be specific to Alice or Bob.

questions.q: In elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman, what does A = a * G mean?
choices: The curve point G added to itself a times
G raised to the power a, modulo a prime
The integer a multiplied by the x-coordinate of G
G hashed a times
questions.explain: a * G is a point on the curve, obtained by adding the public point G to itself a times.

questions.q: What shared secret do Alice and Bob end up with in elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman?
choices: S = a * B = b * A = a * b * G
S = A + B
S = (a + b) * G
S = G^(ab) mod p
questions.explain: Alice computes a * B = a * b * G and Bob computes b * A = b * a * G. Both get the same point. Eve sees only A and B and has no known efficient way to compute S.

questions.q: What is the main practical advantage of elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman over modular-arithmetic Diffie-Hellman?
choices: It achieves the same security with smaller keys
It is secure against man-in-the-middle attacks
It doesn't need any public parameters
Its underlying math is simpler
questions.explain: ECDH reaches the same security with much smaller keys, for example a 256-bit curve versus a 2048-bit prime. The math is more complicated, and ECDH is still vulnerable to MITM without authentication.

questions.q: Which three problems are believed to be roughly equally hard?
choices: Discrete log modulo a 2048-bit prime, elliptic-curve discrete log on a 256-bit curve, and brute-forcing a 128-bit symmetric key
Discrete log modulo a 256-bit prime, elliptic-curve discrete log on a 256-bit curve, and brute-forcing a 256-bit symmetric key
Discrete log modulo a 2048-bit prime, elliptic-curve discrete log on a 2048-bit curve, and brute-forcing a 2048-bit symmetric key
Discrete log modulo a 128-bit prime, elliptic-curve discrete log on a 256-bit curve, and brute-forcing a 2048-bit symmetric key
questions.explain: A 2048-bit prime, a 256-bit curve, and a 128-bit symmetric key give roughly equal security. Brute-forcing the 128-bit key is believed to be slightly harder.

questions.q: You are using 128-bit AES and want the other parts of the system to be about equally hard to break. Which choice fits?
choices: SHA-256 with a 256-bit elliptic curve or a 2048-bit prime for Diffie-Hellman
SHA-256 with a 128-bit prime for Diffie-Hellman
SHA-384 with a 2048-bit elliptic curve
A 128-bit hash with a 4096-bit elliptic curve
questions.explain: Security levels are matched so no single piece is the weak link. 128-bit AES is usually paired with SHA-256 and either 256-bit ECDH or 2048-bit DH.

questions.q: Among discrete log modulo a 2048-bit prime, elliptic-curve discrete log on a 256-bit curve, and brute-forcing a 128-bit key, brute-forcing the 128-bit key is believed to be slightly harder than the other two.
questions.explain: All three are roughly equal in difficulty, and the 128-bit symmetric brute force is believed to be slightly harder.

questions.q: Basic Diffie-Hellman is secure against which kind of adversary?
choices: A passive eavesdropper, but not an active man-in-the-middle
An active man-in-the-middle, but not a passive eavesdropper
Both passive and active adversaries
Neither, unless elliptic curves are used
questions.explain: Eve, who only watches, can't get the key. Mallory, who can tamper with messages, can set up a separate key with each side.

questions.q: Mallory intercepts Alice's g^a mod p and sends Bob g^m mod p instead, where m is Mallory's secret. What key does Bob compute?
choices: g^(mb) mod p
g^(ab) mod p
g^(am) mod p
g^m mod p
questions.explain: Bob raises the value he received to his secret: (g^m)^b = g^(mb) mod p. Mallory can compute the same key as (g^b)^m.

questions.q: Toy MITM: p = 11, g = 2, Alice's a = 3, Bob's b = 4. Mallory picks m = 2 and replaces both A and B with g^m mod p. What key does Bob end up with?
questions.explain: g^m = 2^2 = 4. Bob computes 4^b = 4^4 = 256 mod 11 = 3. Mallory computes the same key from Bob's real B = 5: 5^2 = 25 mod 11 = 3. Alice's key is 4^3 mod 11 = 9, so Alice and Bob no longer share a key.

questions.q: After a successful man-in-the-middle attack on Diffie-Hellman, what can Mallory do?
choices: Decrypt messages Alice sends
Change messages and re-encrypt them under Bob's key before forwarding
Compute the key Bob thinks he shares with Alice
Recover Alice's secret exponent a
questions.explain: Mallory knows g^(am) and g^(bm), so she can decrypt, modify, and re-encrypt traffic in both directions without being noticed. Finding a itself would still mean solving the discrete log problem.

questions.q: What is the root cause of Diffie-Hellman's vulnerability to man-in-the-middle attacks?
choices: The exchanged values have no integrity or authenticity
The discrete log problem is easy for active attackers
The prime p is public
The shared secret is not hashed before use
questions.explain: Nothing proves that the g^x value Bob receives actually came from Alice, so Mallory can swap in her own.

questions.q: How can Alice and Bob defend against a man-in-the-middle during Diffie-Hellman?
choices: Protect the exchanged messages with a scheme that gives integrity and authenticity, such as digital signatures
Use a larger prime p
Switch to elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman
Hash the shared secret before using it
questions.explain: With authenticated messages, Alice and Bob can detect Mallory's tampering. Larger parameters, ECDH, or hashing S don't stop an active attacker.
